questions.stem: Prolonged heating of glucose with hydrogen iodide gives n-hexane. This observation shows that glucose contains:
options: a branched chain of six carbon atoms
a straight chain of six carbon atoms
an aromatic ring of six carbon atoms
questions.explanation: Complete reduction of glucose by HI gives the unbranched alkane n-hexane, so all six carbon atoms must be joined in a single straight chain with no branching. The ring forms later through the hemiacetal link, which involves oxygen and does not change the carbon skeleton.

optionRationale.1: The carbon skeleton is open and unbranched; the ring in the cyclic form includes an oxygen atom.
optionRationale.2: A branched skeleton would have given an isomer such as 2-methylpentane instead of n-hexane.
optionRationale.4: Glucose is an aliphatic polyhydroxy aldehyde, not an aromatic compound.

questions.objective: Use the HI reduction of glucose as evidence for its structure

questions.stem: Lactose, the sugar present in milk, is a disaccharide made up of:
questions.explanation: Lactose is formed from one unit of beta-D-galactose and one unit of beta-D-glucose joined through a C1 to C4 beta-glycosidic linkage. It is therefore a reducing sugar, because the glucose unit keeps a free anomeric carbon.

optionRationale.1: Two alpha-D-glucose units joined by an alpha-1,4 link make maltose.
optionRationale.2: Fructose is not a component of lactose; it occurs in sucrose.
optionRationale.4: Alpha-D-glucose with beta-D-fructose are the two units of sucrose.

questions.objective: Recall the composition of lactose

questions.stem: Night blindness is caused by the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is needed to form the visual pigment in the retina, so its shortage makes it hard to see in dim light, a condition called night blindness. Severe deficiency also causes xerophthalmia, a hardening of the cornea.

optionRationale.1: Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy.
optionRationale.2: Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
optionRationale.3: Vitamin B1 deficiency leads to beriberi, not a vision disorder.

questions.objective: Match a vitamin with its deficiency disease

questions.stem: Which of the following is known as animal starch?
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals and is stored mainly in the liver and muscles. Its structure is similar to amylopectin but is more highly branched, so it is often called animal starch.

optionRationale.1: Amylose is an unbranched component of plant starch, not an animal storage form.
optionRationale.3: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls.
optionRationale.4: Sucrose is a disaccharide, not a polysaccharide.

questions.objective: Identify glycogen as the reserve carbohydrate of animals

questions.stem: A nucleotide is made up of:
options: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group
a nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar only
a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group only
a pentose sugar and a phosphate group only
questions.explanation: A nucleoside is a base attached to a pentose sugar. When a phosphoric acid group is esterified to the sugar of a nucleoside, a nucleotide results. Nucleotides are the repeating units joined into the chains of DNA and RNA.

optionRationale.2: Base plus sugar without phosphate is only a nucleoside.
optionRationale.3: The sugar is the link between base and phosphate, so it cannot be left out.
optionRationale.4: A nucleotide always contains a base, so sugar and phosphate alone are not enough.

questions.objective: Distinguish a nucleotide from a nucleoside

questions.stem: The hormone thyroxine is produced by the:
questions.explanation: Thyroxine is an iodine-containing hormone secreted by the thyroid gland. It controls the basal metabolic rate, and a shortage of iodine in the diet can lead to enlargement of the gland, known as goitre.

optionRationale.1: The pituitary secretes hormones such as growth hormone, not thyroxine.
optionRationale.3: The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon.
optionRationale.4: The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline and corticosteroids.

questions.objective: Recall the source of thyroxine

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
questions.explanation: Fibrous proteins have long thread-like polypeptide chains held side by side by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, and are insoluble in water. Keratin of hair, nails and wool and myosin of muscle are examples.

optionRationale.1: Albumin of egg white is a globular, water-soluble protein.
optionRationale.2: Haemoglobin is a globular protein made of four folded subunits.
optionRationale.3: Insulin is a small globular protein hormone.

questions.objective: Classify proteins as fibrous or globular

questions.stem: Which of the following is an essential amino acid for humans?
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in the human body and must be obtained from the diet. Valine is one of them. Glycine, alanine and proline can be made by the body and are non-essential.

optionRationale.1: Glycine is synthesised in the body, so it is non-essential.
optionRationale.3: Alanine is non-essential; the body makes it.
optionRationale.4: Proline is also manufactured by the body and is non-essential.

questions.objective: Recall an essential amino acid

questions.stem: The alpha and beta forms of D-glucopyranose differ only in the configuration at carbon number 1. Such a pair of cyclic stereoisomers is called:
questions.explanation: When glucose cyclises, C-1 becomes a new chiral centre, and the two possible arrangements of the hydroxyl group at this carbon give the alpha and beta forms. Stereoisomers differing only at the anomeric carbon are called anomers.

optionRationale.1: There is no double bond or ring restriction giving cis-trans isomerism here.
optionRationale.2: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, and these two forms differ at a single carbon, so they are not mirror images.
optionRationale.3: Epimers differing at C-4 would be glucose and galactose, not the alpha and beta forms.

questions.objective: Define anomers and the anomeric carbon

questions.stem: In an electric field, alanine is dissolved in a solution whose pH is higher than its isoelectric point. The amino acid exists mainly as:
options: an anion and moves towards the anode
a zwitterion and does not move
a cation and moves towards the cathode
a neutral molecule with no ionic groups
questions.explanation: Above the isoelectric point the solution has fewer hydrogen ions than the zwitterion needs, so the ammonium group loses a proton while the carboxylate stays ionised. The net charge is negative and the amino acid migrates towards the positive electrode, the anode.

optionRationale.2: The zwitterion with zero net charge exists only at the isoelectric point.
optionRationale.3: The cation forms in solutions with pH below the isoelectric point.
optionRationale.4: Amino acids carry charged groups in water; an uncharged form is not the main species.

questions.objective: Predict the charge of an amino acid relative to its pI

questions.stem: Glycine has a molar mass of $75\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. The molar mass of a pentapeptide made only of glycine units (take water as $18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) is:
questions.explanation: Five glycine units are joined by four peptide bonds, and each bond formation removes one water molecule. The molar mass is therefore $5\times 75-4\times 18 = 375-72 = 303\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

optionRationale.1: 375 is the sum of five glycine units with no water subtracted.
optionRationale.3: 285 subtracts five water molecules, but five units form only four peptide bonds.
optionRationale.4: 321 subtracts only three water molecules instead of four.

questions.objective: Calculate the molar mass of a peptide from its amino acids

questions.stem: The alpha-helix of a protein is stabilised mainly by:
options: hydrogen bonds between amino acid side chains and water
hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide unit and the N-H of another unit in the same chain
ionic bonds between different polypeptide chains
questions.explanation: In the alpha-helix, the polypeptide chain coils into a right-handed spiral, and each carbonyl oxygen forms a hydrogen bond with an amide hydrogen a few residues along the same chain. These repeated hydrogen bonds hold the helical secondary structure.

optionRationale.1: Interaction with water is not what holds the helix; the bonds are within the backbone.
optionRationale.3: Ionic interactions between chains contribute to tertiary and quaternary structure, not to the helix itself.
optionRationale.4: Disulphide bridges are covalent links of tertiary structure.

questions.objective: Identify the forces stabilising secondary structure

questions.stem: Complete hydrolysis of $3.42\,\text{g}$ of sucrose (molar mass $342\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) gives glucose and fructose, each of molar mass $180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. The total mass of the two monosaccharides formed is:
questions.explanation: The amount of sucrose is $3.42/342=0.0100$ mol. Each mole gives one mole of glucose and one of fructose, so $0.0200$ mol of monosaccharide is formed, which weighs $0.0200\times180=3.60\,\text{g}$. The extra $0.18\,\text{g}$ comes from the water used in hydrolysis.

optionRationale.1: 3.42 g ignores the mass of water taken up in hydrolysis.
optionRationale.3: 1.80 g is the mass of glucose alone, not both sugars.
optionRationale.4: 3.78 g wrongly adds the water mass to the product mass a second time.

questions.objective: Apply mole calculations to hydrolysis of sucrose

questions.stem: The blue colour given by starch with iodine is mainly due to:
options: iodine molecules trapped inside the helical coil of amylose
oxidation of the aldehyde group of starch
a covalent bond between iodine and the OH groups of glucose
hydrolysis of starch to glucose by iodine
questions.explanation: The amylose part of starch coils into a helix, and iodine molecules lodge in the hollow of this helix to form a coloured inclusion complex. When starch is hydrolysed or heated strongly the helix breaks and the colour disappears.

optionRationale.2: Starch has no free aldehyde group, and the colour is not an oxidation product.
optionRationale.3: No covalent bond is formed; the colour arises from physical trapping of iodine.
optionRationale.4: Iodine does not hydrolyse starch; acids or enzymes do that.

questions.objective: Explain the iodine test for starch

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction because it:
options: resembles the substrate and occupies the active site of the enzyme
destroys the primary structure of the enzyme
binds to the product and removes it
raises the activation energy of the substrate by heating
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor has a structure close to that of the substrate, so it binds reversibly to the active site and blocks the substrate from entering. The enzyme is not destroyed, and adding more substrate can reduce the effect of the inhibitor.

optionRationale.2: Breaking the primary structure is denaturation by hydrolysis, which is not how competitive inhibition works.
optionRationale.3: The inhibitor acts on the enzyme's active site, not on the product.
optionRationale.4: An inhibitor does not supply heat; it competes for the site.

questions.objective: Describe how enzyme inhibitors act

questions.stem: Pure alpha-D-glucose has a specific rotation of $+111^\circ$ and pure beta-D-glucose has $+19.2^\circ$. At equilibrium in water the mixture shows $+52.5^\circ$. The percentage of the alpha form at equilibrium is closest to:
questions.explanation: Let the fraction of the alpha form be $x$. Then $111x+19.2(1-x)=52.5$, so $91.8x=33.3$ and $x=0.363$, about $36\%$. The beta form is the remainder, about $64\%$, which is why beta-D-glucose is more abundant at equilibrium.

optionRationale.1: 52.5% just reuses the rotation value as a percentage.
optionRationale.3: 48% has no basis in the weighted-average equation.
optionRationale.4: 64% is the beta form, not the alpha form.

questions.objective: Use specific rotations to find composition during mutarotation

questions.stem: The cyclic pyranose form of D-glucose has five chiral carbon atoms. The number of possible stereoisomers of this ring structure is:
questions.explanation: Each of the five chiral centres can have two configurations, so the number of stereoisomers is $2^5=32$. In the open chain only four centres exist, giving 16 aldohexoses, and ring closure adds the anomeric centre.

optionRationale.1: 10 results from adding rather than raising 2 to the power of the number of centres.
optionRationale.2: 16 is $2^4$, the count for the open-chain aldohexose with four chiral carbons.
optionRationale.3: 8 is $2^3$ and corresponds to only three chiral carbons.

questions.objective: Count stereoisomers from the number of chiral centres

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains $28\%$ guanine. The percentage of thymine in the same sample is:
questions.explanation: In double-stranded DNA, guanine pairs with cytosine, so cytosine is also 28 percent. Guanine plus cytosine is 56 percent, leaving 44 percent for adenine plus thymine. Since adenine pairs with thymine, each is $44/2=22\%$.

optionRationale.2: 72% would be 100 minus 28 and ignores the two base-pair rules.
optionRationale.3: 28% is the value for guanine and cytosine, not thymine.
optionRationale.4: 44% is adenine plus thymine together.

questions.objective: Apply Chargaff's rules to base composition

questions.stem: Which of the following amino acids has an isoelectric point greater than 7?
questions.explanation: Lysine has an extra amino group in its side chain, so it is a basic amino acid and a higher pH is needed to reach the neutral zwitterion. Its isoelectric point is near 9.7, while glutamic and aspartic acids, with an extra carboxyl group, have values near 3.

optionRationale.1: Glutamic acid is acidic, with an isoelectric point near 3.
optionRationale.2: Glycine is neutral, and its isoelectric point is near 6.
optionRationale.3: Aspartic acid is also acidic, with an isoelectric point near 2.8.

questions.objective: Relate side chains to isoelectric points

questions.stem: Considering all 20 common amino acids and allowing the same amino acid to appear twice, the number of different dipeptides that can be formed is:
questions.explanation: Each of the two positions of a dipeptide can be filled by any of the 20 amino acids, and the order matters because the N-terminal and C-terminal ends are different. The total number is $20\times20=400$.

optionRationale.1: 380 counts ordered pairs of different amino acids but leaves out the 20 with repeated units.
optionRationale.2: 40 is the sum of 20 plus 20, not the product.
optionRationale.4: 190 is the number of unordered pairs of different amino acids, which ignores order and repeats.

questions.objective: Count the possible peptide sequences

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Glucose does not give Schiff's test even though its open-chain form contains an aldehyde group.
**Reason (R):** In solution glucose exists mainly as cyclic hemiacetal forms, so very little free aldehyde is present.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Glucose in water is almost entirely in the ring forms, in which the aldehyde group has become part of a hemiacetal. Only a trace of the open-chain form is present, not enough to restore the pink colour of Schiff's reagent. The reason explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is not just true; it directly accounts for the negative Schiff's test.
optionRationale.3: R is true: glucose does exist chiefly in cyclic forms.
optionRationale.4: A is true; glucose does not respond to Schiff's reagent.

questions.objective: Explain the absence of aldehyde tests in glucose

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Glucose is a reducing sugar.
**Reason (R):** Glucose contains five hydroxyl groups in its molecule.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Glucose reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents because its ring can open to expose a free aldehyde group, which is oxidised to a carboxylic acid. The presence of five hydroxyl groups is a true fact but has no role in the reducing property, so the reason does not explain the assertion.

optionRationale.1: The five OH groups make glucose soluble but do not cause reduction; the free CHO does.
optionRationale.3: R is true, since glucose has five OH groups.
optionRationale.4: A is true, because glucose reduces Tollens' reagent.

questions.objective: Identify why glucose is reducing

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Starch gives a blue colour with iodine solution.
**Reason (R):** Starch is a polymer of beta-D-glucose units joined by beta-1,4 linkages.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The blue colour arises when iodine is trapped in the helical amylose component, so the assertion is correct. However, starch is built from alpha-D-glucose, with alpha-1,4 links in amylose and extra alpha-1,6 branches in amylopectin. The beta-1,4 polymer is cellulose, so the reason is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is not true; starch contains alpha, not beta, glucose.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the blue colour is the standard test for starch.

questions.objective: Distinguish the glucose units of starch and cellulose

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Thymine is present in RNA.
**Reason (R):** In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine as a pyrimidine base.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: RNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil; thymine is found in DNA. Uracil is the pyrimidine of RNA and replaces thymine, which differs only by a methyl group. The assertion is therefore false while the reason is a true statement.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so R cannot be its explanation.
optionRationale.2: A is false; thymine is not a base of RNA.
optionRationale.3: R is true and A is the false statement.

questions.objective: Recall the bases of DNA and RNA

questions.stem: Match the hormone in List-I with its source or function in List-II.

right: I. Prepares the body for emergency, released by the adrenal gland
II. Controls the basal metabolic rate
III. Lowers the blood glucose level
IV. Controls male secondary sexual characters

questions.explanation: Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose. Thyroxine from the thyroid controls the metabolic rate. Adrenaline from the adrenal gland prepares the body for fight or flight. Testosterone from the testes controls male secondary sex characters. Hence A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: Wrong: C belongs with I, not IV and D belongs with IV, not I.
optionRationale.2: Wrong: B belongs with II, not I and C belongs with I, not II.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: B belongs with II, not IV and D belongs with IV, not II.

questions.objective: Match hormones with their functions

questions.stem: Match the level of protein structure in List-I with its description in List-II.

right: I. Overall folding of one polypeptide chain into a three-dimensional shape
II. Association of two or more polypeptide subunits
III. Regular alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet patterns
IV. Sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence. Secondary structure is the regular helix or pleated sheet. Tertiary structure is the folding of a single chain into a compact shape, and quaternary structure is the assembly of several subunits, as in haemoglobin. So A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

optionRationale.2: Wrong: A belongs with IV, not III and B belongs with III, not IV.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: A belongs with IV, not I and C belongs with I, not IV.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: A belongs with IV, not II and D belongs with II, not IV.

questions.objective: Relate each level of protein structure to its description

questions.stem: Match the vitamin in List-I with a good dietary source in List-II.

right: II. Meat, fish, eggs and curd
III. Fish liver oil and carrots

questions.explanation: Vitamin A is found in fish liver oil and carrots, vitamin C in citrus fruits and amla, vitamin K in green leafy vegetables and vitamin B12 in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and curd. The code is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

optionRationale.2: Wrong: B belongs with I, not II and D belongs with II, not I.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: A belongs with III, not I and B belongs with I, not III.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: A belongs with III, not IV and C belongs with IV, not III.

questions.objective: Match vitamins with their sources

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about DNA.
A. Adenine and guanine are the purine bases of DNA.
B. Cytosine and thymine are the pyrimidine bases of DNA.
C. In double-stranded DNA the amount of adenine equals the amount of guanine.
D. Successive nucleotides in a strand are joined by phosphodiester linkages.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines, and cytosine and thymine are the pyrimidines of DNA. Neighbouring nucleotides are connected through phosphodiester bonds between the 3' and 5' positions of sugars. Statement C is false because adenine pairs with thymine, so adenine equals thymine, not guanine.

optionRationale.1: C is false, since the amounts of A and T are equal, not A and G.
optionRationale.2: A is true and C is false, so this option misses B and D.
optionRationale.4: C is false, and it appears in this option.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements about DNA composition and structure

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about vitamins.
A. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.
B. Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and adipose tissue.
C. Vitamins of the B group and vitamin C are water-soluble.
D. Vitamin K is a water-soluble vitamin.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fats and oils and are stored in the liver and fat tissue. Vitamins of the B complex and vitamin C dissolve in water and are largely excreted, so they must be supplied regularly. Statement D is wrong because vitamin K is fat-soluble.

optionRationale.1: D is false, so not all four statements are correct.
optionRationale.2: B is true but D is false, so this option is incomplete and wrong.
optionRationale.4: D is false, because vitamin K is fat-soluble.

questions.objective: Classify vitamins by solubility and storage

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about carbohydrates.
A. Fructose is a ketohexose.
B. Glucose and fructose give different osazones.
C. Lactose is a non-reducing sugar.
D. Maltose is a reducing sugar.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Fructose has a ketone group at C-2 and is a ketohexose. Maltose keeps one free anomeric carbon, so it reduces Tollens' reagent. Glucose and fructose give the same osazone because C-1 and C-2 are converted and the rest of the chain is identical, and lactose is reducing, so B and C are false.

optionRationale.1: B and C are both false.
optionRationale.2: C is false: lactose has a free hemiacetal group of glucose and is reducing.
optionRationale.4: B is false: glucose and fructose give the same osazone.

questions.objective: Evaluate facts about reducing sugars and osazones
